course_description:
Advanced knowledge and understanding of process and engineering principles of various methods of heating, cooling, freezing, drying of foods, crystallisation, extrusion and membrane separation; water relations in foods and kinetics of physico-chemical changes during processing.

To develop advanced knowledge and understanding of process engineering principles of spray drying of foods, food powder properties, crystallisation, extrusion, emulsification and rice processing technologies. In addition, to provide an understanding of the water activity predictionﾠand heat sterilisation of foods. The course will be conducted via lectures, tutorials and practicals.

This course is co-taught with FOOD3008.

At the School of Agriculture and Food Sustainability, we are committed to creating an inclusive and empowering learning environment for all students. We value and respect the diverse range of experiences our students bring to their education, and we believe that this diversity is crucial for fostering a rich culture of knowledge-sharing and meaningful exploration. We hold students and staff accountable for actively contributing to establishing a respectful and supportive learning environment.

Bullying, harassment, and discrimination in any form are strictly against our principles and againstﾠ UQ Policy, ﾠand will not be tolerated. If you have any concerns about your experience in this course, we encourage you to tell a member of the course teaching team. Your well-being and a positive learning atmosphere are of utmost importance to us.

course_aims: To develop an advanced knowledge and understanding of process engineering principles of heating, cooling, cereal processing, drying, powder properties, extrusion, crystallisation, emulsification and water activity control in food. To provide an understanding of the water relations in foods and kinetics of physico-chemical changes during processing and storage.

learning_outcomes.description: Apply the theoretical process engineering principles of unit operations in various food manufacturing processes

Use the engineering principles in various food engineering processes: crystallisation, rice processing, emulsification, spray drying, extrusion and water activity prediction in addressing scenarios in food process engineering
Undertake experiments related to food process engineering to determine both qualitative and quantitative outcomes
Apply food process engineering principles and techniques in collaborative practical sessions and individually analyse and report experimental outcomes.

assessment_details.title: Sequential Practical Assessments - presentations
assessment_details.weight: 40% 2 Presentations weighted at 20% each, for a total of 40%
assessment_details.task_description: Presentations Presentation 1 : Water activity, crystallisation, and Homogenization (20%) Presentation 2 : Rice processing, Packaging, Spray Drying, and Extrusion (DEMO). (20%) A practical presentation (SINGLE student) for each project is to be prepared in a pre-recorded video file and submitted by the due date. The presentation should be 20 minutes in length. Marking criteria (out of 100%): Clarity of Communication (5%) Demonstrates clear and confident explanation of key concepts. Shows strong understanding of both practical sessions and theoretical background. Language is appropriate, engaging, and avoids reading directly from a script. Uses examples or analogies where useful to enhance understanding. Presentation Structure and Flow (5%) Presentation follows a logical structure with a clear introduction, main body, and conclusion. Transitions between sections are smooth, and the overall flow supports audience comprehension. Quality and Relevance of Visuals (10%) Visuals are clear, well-formatted, and directly support the spoken content. Graphs and figures have properly labelled axes, units, and legends. Visuals include relevant equations or illustrations where needed, avoid unnecessary clutter, and limit the number of words. Accuracy and Explanation of Calculations (35%) Calculations and equations are used appropriately, applied correctly, and clearly explained. Shows understanding of what the numbers mean, their relevance to theory, and how they relate to practical observations. Assumptions and limitations are clearly acknowledged. Connection to Lecture Topics (10%) Presentation demonstrates a strong link to key course concepts and lecture material. Uses correct terminology and references core models or frameworks introduced in the course. Shows how the presentation content fits within the broader learning objectives. Timing and Length Management (5%) The presentation stays within the allotted time. Pacing is even, content is covered efficiently, and the speaker maintains control of timing without rushing or finishing too early. Critical Analysis and Real-World Relevance (15%) Demonstrates a critical evaluation of results, methods, and assumptions rather than simple description. Provides clear reasoning to support interpretations, including discussion of limitations, uncertainties, and alternative explanations. Effectively connects findings to real-world applications, industrial contexts, or practical implications. Shows the ability to reflect on how the results can be applied, improved, or extended beyond the practical sessions. Use and Selection of References (15%) At least four credible and relevant scientific references must be used to support the content. These references should be clearly cited and effectively integrated into the discussion to justify methods, results, and interpretations. In addition, for each practical session, one presentation slide should be dedicated to analysing a relevant scientific reference linked to that session. Students may appropriately use AI and/or MT in completing this assessment task. Students must clearly reference and/or acknowledge any use of AI or MT in each instance. Students must submit Assessment task, in Blackboard, via the link by the submission deadline. An electronic copy of every piece of assessment submitted should be retained.
Legal Declaration:
By submitting your work via this website, you formally declare that (1) it is your own original work, and no part of the work has been copied from any other source or person except where due acknowledgement is made; (2) no part of the work has been previously submitted for assessment in this or any other institution; and (3) you have read the UQ Academic Integrity and Plagiarism Policy ( https://policies.uq.edu.au/document/view-current.php?id=149 ) and understand its implications.
Deferral or extension
You may be able to apply for an extension .
The maximum extension allowed is 28 days. Extensions are given in multiples of 24 hours.
Submission of an Extension of Assessment Due Date (EADD) should be completed online through your My Requests tab via my.UQ Dashboard , in accordance with the University's Assessment Procedure (located in the Policies and Procedures section of this course profile) which outlines the requirements for requesting extensions to assessment due dates. Extensions require the correct evidence/documentation to support the requested length of time of the extension.
Late submission
A penalty of 10% of the maximum possible mark will be deducted per 24 hours from time submission is due for up to 7 days. After 7 days, you will receive a mark of 0.
For example, a report worth a maximum of 40 marks, submitted 28 hours late will incur a penalty of 8 marks. This is calculated as 2 (24 hour periods) x 10% per period x 40 marks, resulting in 8 marks deducted from the student’s mark for the assessment.
Assessment deadlines are firm and must be met. Late submission without permission or non-submission of assessable work will result in penalties being applied . Late submission of assessment will only be granted for documented medical reasons, accident, bereavement, jury service and other circumstances allowed in the UQ Policies and Procedures Library (PPL).

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 1 To Week 12 (27 Jul - 25 Oct)
learning_activities.topic: Lectures Delivered lectures covering a range of core food engineering topics, including water activity, sorption property prediction, crystallisation, size reduction, homogenisation and emulsification, particle engineering, spray drying, powder property analysis, rice processing, encapsulation techniques, extrusion, packaging technologies, and alternative processing methods Learning outcomes: L01, L02

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 1 To Week 12 (27 Jul - 25 Oct)
learning_activities.topic: Tutorials Facilitated tutorials involving group-based problem-solving exercises on key food engineering topics, including water activity, sorption isotherms, crystallisation mechanisms, size reduction principles, homogenisation and emulsification dynamics, particle design, spray drying operations, powder characterisation, rice milling, encapsulation strategies, extrusion processes, packaging systems, and alternative processing techniques. Learning outcomes: L02, L03

learning_activities.learning_period: Multiple weeks From Week 1 To Week 12 (27 Jul - 25 Oct)
learning_activities.topic: Practicals Led hands-on practical sessions involving group-based experiments on key food processing techniques, including measurement and analysis of water activity and sorption properties, homogenisation of food emulsions, characterisation of powder properties, spray drying of model formulations, and rice milling and quality assessment. The extrusion process was demonstrated to illustrate principles and equipment operation. Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04
